slides.label: Title
slides.notes: This is the outcome that turns compass work into navigation. Tell them up front that none of it is difficult, but all of it needs practice, and the ones who practise pacing will be the ones who find the checkpoint in fog.
slides.html:
2434 (Church Fenton) Squadron · Air Training Corps
Basic Navigation Using
Map and Compass
Learning Outcome 4
Land navigation methods — measuring, timing, pacing, and the techniques good navigators actually use

slides.label: LO4 statement
slides.notes: Read it out. KNOW rather than BE ABLE TO, so this is assessed by questions - but everything in it is worth practising on the ground anyway.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 4
Know land navigation methods

slides.label: What LO4 covers
slides.notes: Signpost the whole lesson. The four go together: you measure a distance, you predict a time, you count the paces, and the aids stop you needing to be perfect. Say that last part - the aids exist because nobody walks a perfect bearing.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 4
What this outcome covers
One
Measuring distances
On the map, and what that means on the ground.
Two
Timing
How long a leg should take, and using that as a check.
Three
Pacing
Counting your own paces to measure real distance.
Four
Aids to navigation
Seven techniques that make a leg easier to get right.

slides.label: Section: measuring
slides.notes: Signpost part one. Short section, but the slope-distance slide in it surprises everybody.
slides.html:
Part One
Measuring and
pinpointing
Getting a real distance off a map, and using one bearing to place yourself on a path.

slides.label: Roamer recap
slides.notes: Two minutes only - they had this in LO3. Use it as a live test rather than a lecture: give them a feature and time how long it takes the room to produce the same six figures.
slides.html:
Measuring
The roamer, again
A quick recap from the last outcome, because you will use it constantly.
▸Check the roamer matches your map scale
▸Corner of the roamer on the feature
▸Read where the scales cut the grid lines
▸Eastings first, then northings
▸Always the lowest figures, from the south-west corner
Eastings first: 377 067

slides.label: Pinpointing position
slides.notes: The important condition is the one cadets skip: this only works because the path already gives you a line. One bearing plus one known line equals a fix. Ask what they would need if they were not on a path - three bearings, which is resection.
slides.html:
Pinpointing
One bearing, if you know roughly where you are
Pinpointing fixes your position with a single bearing — but only because you already know you are on a line.
▸You are walking the path and know you are on it
▸You are just unsure how far along
▸Take a bearing on the peak
▸Trace that bearing back from the peak on the map
▸Where it cuts the path is roughly where you are
Where the bearing line cuts the path is your position

slides.label: Slope distance
slides.notes: This is the slide that changes how cadets plan. Do the arithmetic with them if anyone asks where 141.4 comes from - it is a right-angled triangle with equal sides. Then ask what that does to a five-kilometre day in the Dales.
slides.html:
Measuring
The map lies about distance
The map is a bird’s-eye view. It measures the ground as if it were flat — and it never is.
▸On the map the leg measures 100 metres.
▸Up the slope you actually walk 141.4 metres.
▸That is 40 per cent more ground than the map admits to.
▸Take the terrain into account when you plan, or every timing you calculate will be optimistic.
100 m on the map, 141.4 m on the ground

slides.label: Dog-leg detours
slides.notes: The discipline is the counting. Cadets happily walk round an obstacle and then guess their way back on, which is how legs go wrong. Make the point that the detour is two known distances, not a wander.
slides.html:
Off the straight line
Dog-leg detours
You will often be unable to walk straight at your destination. A marsh, a boulder field, a ridge — something is always in the way.
▸Work out how far off the straight line you need to go.
▸Time and pace the detour leg.
▸Walk back to the route line by the same amount.
▸If you can, pinpoint your position to confirm you are back on the bearing.
Round the marsh, the boulder and the ridge

slides.label: Spot and line transit
slides.notes: Cadets find this one genuinely satisfying because it costs nothing and needs no compass. Draw a couple on their own extracts before you move on. Point out that the sharpest transits come from features far apart in depth, not side by side.
slides.html:
Off the straight line
Spot and line transits
When two features on the map will line up with each other somewhere along your route, you have a free position check.
▸Draw a line on the map through both features, continuing across your route.
▸As you walk, watch for the two features coming into line on the ground.
▸The moment they line up, you are where that line crosses your route.
▸Linear features work too — extend a wall, a fence or a straight stream on the map to make more transit lines.
Two features in line means one point on your route

slides.label: ANIMATION Staying on the Line
slides.notes: Run this after transits, because it shows them being used as checks rather than as a party trick. Pause on the drifting version and ask how far off the cadet would be after another kilometre.

slides.label: Section: aids
slides.notes: The heart of the outcome. Frame it properly: good navigators do not rely on perfect compass work and perfect measurement, they use technique so that being slightly wrong does not matter.
slides.html:
Part Two
Aids to navigation
Seven techniques. None of them assumes you can walk a perfect bearing — because nobody can.

slides.label: The seven aids
slides.notes: Read the list, do not explain it yet - each gets its own slide. Ask which ones they have used without knowing the name. Handrailing is almost always the answer.
slides.html:
Aids to navigation
The seven
Each one is a way of making a leg forgiving instead of exact.
▸Attack points — go via something you cannot miss
▸Handrailing — follow a linear feature that goes your way
▸Aiming off — miss on purpose, on the side you choose
▸Contouring — round the hill instead of over it
▸Boxing round — get past an obstacle and back on line
▸Mapping spiral — search when you are close but blind
▸Outriggers — use the team to hold the bearing straight

slides.label: Attack points
slides.notes: The insight is that a longer route can be more accurate than a shorter one. Cadets resist this because it looks inefficient. Point out that the final leg from the attack point is short, so the error on it is small.
slides.html:
Aid one
Attack points
An easily identified feature close enough to your objective that you can home in from it.
▸It pays to go slightly out of your way to hit something definite.
▸From point A, aim for where the stream enters the lake — you cannot miss that.
▸Then make the short move onto point B.
▸Try for B in one leg and a small error means you miss it altogether.
Via the stream mouth, then onto B

slides.label: Using attack points
slides.notes: Walk them through it on the diagram in order. The key comparison is the length of the final leg in each version - that is where the error lives. Ask what the attack point would be if there were no wood.
slides.html:
Aid one
Attack points in practice
From the start point, going straight for the hut is the risky option.
▸Mist comes down, you veer slightly right, you miss the hut entirely.
▸Instead: aim for the wood — a big target you will hit.
▸At the wood, turn right and follow the edge to its corner.
▸From the corner, set your course for the hut. A far shorter leg, so far less chance of missing.
Wood, then corner of the wood, then hut

slides.label: Handrailing
slides.notes: This is the one they already do instinctively. The tributary warning is the teaching point - a stream junction in poor visibility is exactly where people go wrong, and a two-second compass check prevents it.
slides.html:
Aid two
Handrailing
Follow a linear feature that happens to go where you want. A path, a wall, a river, a ridge, a line of pylons.
▸From position A: edge of the wood to the stream.
▸Stream to the power line.
▸Power line to the path.
▸Path to the campsite. No bearings needed at all.
Watch out
Handrailing a stream, do not get taken up a tributary. Check the general direction against your compass.
Four handrails, one route

slides.label: Aiming off
slides.notes: Get the logic out loud: aiming at the target gives a 50/50 guess, aiming off gives certainty. Ask which side they would choose and why - usually the side with the easier ground or the shorter walk back.
slides.html:
Aid three
Aiming off
You are at A and want the bridge. Aim straight at it and you may miss — and in poor visibility you will not know whether to turn upstream or down.
▸So do not aim at the bridge.
▸Deliberately aim off to one side.
▸Now when you hit the river you know exactly which way to turn.
▸A deliberate error you can correct beats an accidental one you cannot.
Aim off, hit the river, turn the way you know

slides.label: Aiming off 2
slides.notes: Second example so the pattern rather than the picture sticks. Ask the room to state the rule in one sentence before you move on.
slides.html:
Aid three
Aiming off again
The same trick, this time for a river junction
From the hill top to the river junction — identical reasoning. Aim off, hit the river, and walk up or down knowing which.

slides.label: Contouring
slides.notes: Hold this diagram in mind - you come back to it at the end of the lesson for the Naismith exercise. The phrase to teach is collecting feature: something across your line that you cannot walk past without noticing.
slides.html:
Aid four
Contouring
Round the hill, or up and over? The two routes may take the same time, but contouring takes less effort.
▸Your navigation has to be good — especially in poor visibility.
▸There is a natural tendency to lose height and to drift too far round the curve.
▸It helps to aim for a collecting feature, like the stream at B, that stops you overshooting.
Round the spur, collected by the stream at B

slides.label: Boxing round
slides.notes: The whole technique hangs on step one and step three being the same count. Do it in the hall or the car park - four right angles and see who comes back on the line. It also proves why pacing matters.
slides.html:
Aid five
Boxing round an obstacle
1On the bearing, at the obstacle: turn 90° left, walk until you are past the end of it, counting your paces.
2Turn 90° right, back onto the original bearing, and walk past the obstacle. The count here does not matter much.
3Turn 90° right and walk back the same number of paces you counted in step one.
4Turn 90° left. You are on your original line again.
Four right angles, one counted distance

slides.label: Mapping spiral
slides.notes: One visibility means how far you can actually see right now - twenty metres in fog, two hundred on a clear day. That is what makes the method work in any conditions. Trace the route on the diagram so they see the coverage.
slides.html:
Aid six
The mapping spiral
For when you know you are close to your marker but cannot see it — or have nothing at all to orient on.
▸From where you are, walk in a chosen direction — say north — for one visibility.
▸Turn east and walk two visibilities.
▸Then south for three, and so on.
▸There is no point on the grid that cannot be seen from somewhere on that route.
Also useful
If you are lost with nothing to identify, keep spiralling until you find a feature you can name.
An expanding square search

slides.label: Outriggers
slides.notes: Best taught outside with three cadets and the rest watching. The signals need to be unambiguous because you will be using them when you cannot hear each other. It also gives the least confident cadet a real job in the middle.
slides.html:
Aid seven
Outriggers
Three people minimum, two of whom must be navigators. This is how you hold a bearing genuinely straight over distance.
▸Everyone sets the same bearing.
▸The strongest navigator leads on that bearing.
▸The second follows in the leader’s footsteps, 10–15 metres back.
▸The third, a navigator, follows checking their own compass and watching whether the two ahead are in line.
▸The leader stops at regular distances; everyone else stops at once.
▸On line: the rear person raises one arm. Off line: they point left or right with an outstretched arm.
▸When corrected, the rear raises both arms; the leader raises both to acknowledge; everyone walks on.

slides.notes: The longest animation in the set at about three minutes. Run it as consolidation for the whole section rather than stopping at each technique. Then ask which one they would use for the specific ground you next take them onto.

slides.label: Section: errors
slides.notes: This section is what makes cadets take the rest seriously. Do not soften the numbers.
slides.html:
Part Three
How errors grow
A small mistake at the start is a big mistake a kilometre later.

slides.label: Area of uncertainty
slides.notes: Let the diagram do the work before you give the figures. Ask them to guess how big the uncertainty is after a kilometre, then give them the answer on the next slide. The guesses are always far too small.
slides.html:
Errors
Your area of uncertainty
It gets large after a remarkably short distance
Every method of estimating distance has an error attached. Add the error in measuring direction and it compounds fast.

slides.label: The arithmetic of error
slides.notes: The three lessons at the bottom are the examinable part. Say them slowly. The deeper point is that short legs are the single most effective fix, because the error is proportional to distance - two legs of 500 metres beat one of a kilometre.
slides.html:
Errors
Four football pitches, then thirty-six
Assume a fairly generous ±10% error in distance and ±4° in direction — realistic for a new navigator.
▸After 1 km, the area you might be in is about four football pitches.
▸After 3 km, it is thirty-six football pitches.
▸The error does not add up. It multiplies.
So
Keep the legs short. Practise your compass work until bearings are accurate. Practise pacing and timing until distance is accurate.

slides.label: Degree error
slides.notes: Six degrees is nothing on a compass dial - show them how small it looks. That is the point. Then connect it to the metal warning from LO3: a watch or a knife near the compass will move the needle by more than six degrees.
slides.html:
Errors
Six degrees is 156 metres
A small error in the bearing has consequences over a surprisingly short distance.
▸A 6° error, walked for 1.5 km
▸Puts you 156 metres off course
▸At 3 km/h that is half an hour’s walking
▸Which is one and a half football pitches off
▸And six degrees is easy to be out by
A 6° error over 1.5 km puts you 156 m off line

slides.label: ANIMATION How Errors Grow
slides.notes: Run this to close the section. Watching the cone open is far more persuasive than the football-pitch figures. Stop it at one kilometre and again at three.

slides.label: Section: timing
slides.notes: Last section. Frame Naismith as a starting point they will personalise, not a law.
slides.html:
Part Four
Timing
Naismith’s Rule — a rough plan is better than no plan.

slides.label: Naismiths Rule
slides.notes: Work an example on the board with the room: four kilometres flat with 300 metres of climb. Forty-eight minutes plus thirty, so about an hour and twenty. Then stress the personalisation - a cadet with a heavy bergen is not doing 5 km/h and should know it.
slides.html:
Timing
Naismith’s Rule
A formula for working out roughly how long a hill route will take.
▸One hour for every 5 km walked on the flat.
▸One hour for every 600 m of ascent — which is 10 minutes per 100 m, or 10 m per minute.
▸Use the same value for downhill as for the flat.
Make it yours
Every walk and every walker is different. Start with Naismith, then adjust — 4 km/h if that fits you better. Whatever numbers you use, you have a plan.
5 km per hour, plus an hour per 600 m of climb

slides.label: ANIMATION Naismiths Rule
slides.notes: Run this straight after the rule so the arithmetic is visible rather than abstract. Then set them a route of their own to time.
slides.html:
Animation · play now
Naismith’s Rule
A route profile with the flat distance and the ascent split out, the two allowances added, and the total time assembled step by step.

slides.label: Speed and distance
slides.notes: The practical use is the running check: if the leg should take twelve minutes and you have been walking twenty, stop - you are not where you think you are. That habit finds errors early, while they are still small.
slides.html:
Timing
Speed and distance
What a given pace actually covers
Knowing your own speed turns a timing into a position check.

slides.label: Exercise: contouring
slides.notes: Let them do it in pairs with pencils. The answer depends on the height gain, which is the lesson - the short route is not automatically the fast one, and the fast route is not automatically the easy one. Finish by asking which they would pick in poor visibility, where contouring needs much better navigation.
slides.html:
Exercise
Contouring or over the top?
Back to the contouring diagram. Work out both routes from A to B using Naismith’s Rule.
▸Route 1 — contouring: round the spur, 4 km.
▸Route 2 — over the hill: 2 km, but with the climb.
▸How long does each take? Which would you choose, and why?
4 km round, or 2 km over

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Round the room. If they can only name two aids, go back to the seven-item list - naming them is the assessable part. The 156 metres figure is worth committing to memory because it makes the case for short legs on its own.
slides.html:

2

4
State Naismith’s Rule.
